title: JavaScript Objects Applied Check
description: Test your ability to predict object reference behavior, JSON conversion, shallow copying, nested updates, and applied object patterns.
author: DailyCoder

questions.explanation: `admin` and `user` reference the same object, so changing one reference changes the shared object.

questions.prompt:
What does this code log?
```js
console.log({ name: "Alice" } === { name: "Alice" });
```

options.text: `true`, because the objects have the same properties
`false`, because they are two different object references

questions.explanation: Objects are compared by reference, not by matching contents.
The spread update creates a new object. The original `user.role` remains `"user"`.
Spread order matters. The later `...user` overwrites the earlier `role: "admin"`.
Object spread is shallow. The nested `address` object is still shared between `user` and `copy`.

questions.prompt: Which update copies nested object data correctly without changing the original city?
questions.explanation: To update nested data immutably, copy the top-level object and the nested object being changed.

options.text: A deep copy of all nested data
A shallow copy of the top-level object

questions.explanation: Object spread creates a new top-level object, but nested objects remain shared references.

questions.prompt: What does `const json = JSON.stringify({ name: "Alice" });` store in `json`?
questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify()` converts a JavaScript value into a JSON string.
JSON requires double quotes around property names and string values, and it does not support `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What happens when `JSON.parse()` receives invalid JSON?
questions.explanation: `JSON.parse()` expects valid JSON text. Invalid JSON throws a `SyntaxError`.
JSON does not represent `undefined` or functions, so those properties are omitted during stringification.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(object))` for deep copying?

options.text: It only works on arrays, not objects
It loses JSON-unsafe values like functions, `undefined`, and `Date` objects
It always mutates the original object

questions.explanation: JSON-based deep copying only preserves JSON-compatible data and loses several JavaScript-specific value types.

options.text: Always throws a syntax error before running

questions.explanation: `Object.freeze()` prevents top-level property changes. In strict mode, the assignment may throw, but the value does not change.
`json` is a string, not an object. It does not have a `name` property containing `Alice`.

questions.prompt: Which function updates a user's role without mutating the original object?

options.text: `function promote(user) { const next = user; next.role = "admin"; return next; }`

questions.explanation: Returning `{ ...user, role: "admin" }` creates a new object with the updated role and leaves the original object unchanged.
